glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 8 lets Wisdom speak for herself: she calls to everyone in public, names the truth and just rule she brings, and reveals that she was with the LORD before and during creation, so that whoever finds her finds life.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: The chapter follows the seductress who met one young man at night (7:6–27) and opens the prologue’s last movement, where Wisdom and Folly issue rival invitations (8:1–9:18).

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “For whoever finds me finds life, And obtains favor from the LORD” (Proverbs 8:35)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 8 answers chapter 7 on purpose. The seductress waited for one young man “In the twilight” (7:9), but Wisdom stands “Beside the way, where the paths meet” and at the city gates, calling, “To you, O men, I call” (8:2–4). Wisdom, the skill of living life God’s way, hides nothing and flatters no one. Her words hold “Nothing crooked or perverse” (8:8), and she offers them even to the simple and to fools (8:5).

Then the poem reaches back before time. Wisdom was “established from everlasting” (8:23), older than the depths, the mountains, and “the primal dust of the world” (8:26). When the LORD prepared the heavens and gave the sea its limit, she was “beside Him as a master craftsman” and “daily His delight” (8:30), and her own delight was in the human race (8:31). The voice at the crossroads belongs to the one who stood beside the Creator while He made the world.

In the poem Wisdom is a noble woman. In the light of the New Testament, this portrait reveals the eternal Son. Paul calls Christ “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and John says of the Word, “All things were made through Him” (John 1:3). The Son is uncreated, for He “was in the beginning with God” (John 1:2), and Wisdom’s promise, “whoever finds me finds life” (8:35), is fulfilled in the One who is the life (John 14:6).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 8:1–11 — Wisdom’s Open Call

Where the seductress met one young man in the dark, Wisdom raises her voice at the places where travelers must choose a road, and she addresses even the simple and fools. She asks for a hearing because her words hold nothing twisted, and she sets her instruction above the finest silver and gold (8:10–11).

Proverbs 8:12–21 — Wisdom’s Character and Rule

Wisdom introduces her companions, prudence, knowledge, and discretion, and names what she hates, beginning with pride, because the fear of the LORD is to hate evil. Every ruler who governs justly depends on her, and those who love and seek her receive lasting goods that come along the paths of righteousness, not a guarantee of easy wealth.

Proverbs 8:22–26 — Before the World Began

Wisdom now speaks of her origin: she belonged to the LORD at the beginning of His way, before the ocean depths, the mountains, or the first dust of the earth existed. Since this Wisdom is revealed as the eternal Son, her being “brought forth” (8:24–25) may be connected with His eternal relation to the Father, but never with a start to His existence.

Proverbs 8:27–31 — Beside Him at Creation

As the LORD set the heavens in place, drew a circle on the deep, and fixed the boundary of the sea, Wisdom was at His side, working with Him and rejoicing before Him day after day. Her joy reaches past the mountains and seas to the people who would live in His world.

Proverbs 8:32–36 — Whoever Finds Me Finds Life

With “Now therefore,” Wisdom turns everything she has revealed into a reason to listen now, and she pictures the blessed person waiting each day at her doors. The chapter ends at a fork in the road: finding her brings life and the LORD’s favor, while hating her is loving death.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 8 gives the book’s practical counsel its authority. The one who tells the simple to hate pride and speak truth stood beside the LORD as He gave the sea its limit, “So that the waters would not transgress His command” (8:29). Living God’s way means living by the design of the world He made, and the Christ who calls through Wisdom is the One through whom that world was made.

The chapter also shows how open and how serious the call is. Wisdom names the simple and fools, and she promises, “I love those who love me, And those who seek me diligently will find me” (8:17), words heard at the deeper level as Christ’s own. Turning away from her is never a neutral choice, since “he who sins against me wrongs his own soul” (8:36).

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Wisdom’s open call. Wisdom speaks in public at the hilltop, the crossroads, and the city gates, while the seductress of chapter 7 worked in the dark (8:1–5; 7:9).

The fear of the LORD and the hatred of evil. A right view of God hates pride, arrogance, the evil way, and the perverse mouth, and Wisdom hates the same things (8:13).

Riches that last. Wisdom’s instruction outranks silver, gold, and rubies, and the riches with her are joined to righteousness. They describe the lasting fruit of loving wisdom rather than a promise of wealth to everyone (8:10–11, 18–21).

Wisdom and just rule. Kings, princes, nobles, and judges who govern rightly do so by her, so every just ruler depends on a wisdom he did not invent (8:15–16).

Life and death. The chapter closes with two outcomes: life and the LORD’s favor for those who find Wisdom, and death for those who hate her (8:35–36).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Wisdom (8:1, 12). Skill for living life God’s way. Here Wisdom speaks in the first person, “I, wisdom” (8:12). The Hebrew word is feminine, so the poem speaks of Wisdom as she and her; this is the language of poetry, and it never makes Wisdom a goddess or Christ feminine.

The simple and fools (8:5). The simple are uncommitted and easily led, and fools are morally deficient, not merely slow to learn. Wisdom calls both, urging the simple to understand prudence and fools to gain “an understanding heart.”

Prudence and discretion (8:5, 12). Prudence is practical good sense, and discretion is the ability to plan a wise course. Wisdom says she dwells with prudence, so where she is, sound judgment is found as well.

Possessed (8:22). The NKJV word describes Wisdom as belonging to the LORD “at the beginning of His way,” and the next verse places this “from everlasting” (8:23). Because this Wisdom is revealed as the eternal Son, the verse never means that He was created or had a beginning (John 1:1–3; Colossians 1:17).

Master craftsman (8:30). The NKJV’s rendering of a rare Hebrew word whose exact sense is debated. The picture is of Wisdom at the Creator’s side as the world was made, sharing His work and His joy, and the New Testament says the Father “made the worlds” through His Son (Hebrews 1:2).

Obtains favor from the LORD (8:35). The LORD’s approval and kindness. The same words return in 18:22, “He who finds a wife finds a good thing, And obtains favor from the LORD,” which prepares for the question “Who can find a virtuous wife?” (31:10) and links Wisdom found at the start of the book with the bride found at its end.

outline: Proverbs 8:32–36 — Whoever Finds Me Finds Life

1.brief: The chapter opens with a question that expects a yes: “Does not wisdom cry out”? Wisdom and understanding lift their voice openly, in sharp contrast to the seductress of chapter 7, who whispered her offer in the dark.
1.explain:
“Does not wisdom cry out,”

The chapter opens with a question that expects the answer yes. In 8:1–3 the speaker describes Wisdom before she speaks for herself from 8:4 onward. The question comes immediately after chapter 7, which ended at “the chambers of death” (7:27). The seductress spoke in the dark to one young man; now the reader is asked to notice that Wisdom has been calling all along, openly and loudly. No one can claim that her voice was hidden.

“And understanding lift up her voice?”

Understanding stands beside wisdom as her partner, the ability to see into things and grasp what is true. Both raise their voice so that it carries. The poem speaks of wisdom as a woman because the Hebrew word for wisdom is feminine and because the book sets Wisdom opposite the immoral woman of chapters 5–7. The feminine language belongs to the poetry. It does not present Wisdom as a goddess, and it does not make Christ feminine. In the book’s fuller reading, which the New Testament makes possible, the Wisdom who speaks in this chapter is the eternal Son of God, whom Paul calls “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). The chapter first lets her speak in her own poetic portrait, and that portrait must be heard on its own terms before its deeper meaning is drawn out.
1.notes: 8:1–3 describe Wisdom in the third person; from 8:4 to the end of the chapter she speaks in the first person.

2.brief: Wisdom takes her stand on the top of the high hill, beside the road where the paths meet. She places herself where she can be seen and heard, at the very spot where travelers must choose which way to go.
2.explain:
“She takes her stand on the top of the high hill,”

Wisdom chooses the most visible place in the landscape. On a hilltop she can be seen and heard from far away. The seductress lurked at corners and waited for darkness, as 7:9–12 described; Wisdom stands in the open and in the light.

“Beside the way, where the paths meet.”

She also stands beside the road, at the crossroads, the place where travelers must decide which way to go. That is exactly where the young man of chapter 7 went wrong, when he “took the path to her house” (7:8). Wisdom places herself at the point of decision, before the turn is made and not after the damage is done. The book’s two ways, one leading to life and one to death, meet at this spot, and Wisdom is waiting there.

3.brief: She also cries out by the city gates and at the entrances of the doors. Wisdom goes where people come and go, so no one can say her call was hidden from them.
3.explain:
“She cries out by the gates, at the entry of the city,”

The city gate was the busiest public place in an ancient town. Elders sat there to judge cases, merchants traded, and everyone coming in or going out passed through. Wisdom calls where the life of the community is carried on, as she did in chapter 1, “At the openings of the gates in the city” (1:21).

“At the entrance of the doors:”

Her call continues “At the entrance of the doors,” the doorways at the city’s entry where people pass in and out. From the hilltop to the crossroads to the city gate, Wisdom takes her stand wherever people come and go, so that no one can say her call was out of reach. The colon at the end of the line introduces her own words.

4.brief: Wisdom now speaks in her own voice: “To you, O men, I call,” and her voice goes out to the sons of men. Her call is for everyone, and at the deeper level of the book it is the voice of Christ calling all people to Himself.
4.explain:
“To you, O men, I call,”

Now Wisdom speaks in the first person, and her speech continues to the end of the chapter. “To you” is direct and personal. “O men” addresses people simply as people. She does not wait for her hearers to become wise, important or religious before she speaks to them.

“And my voice is to the sons of men.”

“The sons of men” means human beings, the whole human race. The phrase returns at the climax of the creation poem, where Wisdom says, “my delight was with the sons of men” (8:31). She calls the human race because she delights in it. In the light of the New Testament this is the voice of Christ calling all people to Himself; Jesus Himself spoke of “the wisdom of God” sending messengers (Luke 11:49). That deeper reading does not erase the plain portrait of a noble woman calling in public. The portrait is the picture through which the deeper meaning is seen.

5.brief: She addresses the simple and the fools by name, urging the simple to understand prudence and fools to gain an understanding heart. Wisdom’s offer reaches even those who have so far ignored her, which shows her call is full of hope.
5.explain:
“O you simple ones, understand prudence,”

Wisdom names her hearers. The simple are the uncommitted, easily led and not yet settled in wisdom, like the young man of 7:7. She calls them to understand prudence, the practical good sense that sees danger coming and acts in time. Prudence is exactly what the young man of chapter 7 lacked when he wandered toward her corner.

“And you fools, be of an understanding heart.”

She also calls fools, who in Proverbs are morally deficient and resistant to instruction, not merely slow. She urges them to gain an understanding heart, inner sense and judgment. Wisdom’s offer reaches even those who have so far ignored her, and she begins with the least promising hearers. Her call is full of hope. The heart that the young man of 7:7 lacked is the very thing she offers.
5.notes: In Hebrew “be of an understanding heart” reads literally ‘understand heart,’ with the same verb Wisdom uses in the first line for “understand prudence.” Here “heart” means inner sense and judgment, which is why the ESV has “learn sense” and the NASB “understand wisdom.”

6.brief: Wisdom asks for a hearing because she will speak excellent things, and right things will come from her lips. Her words are noble and upright, worth stopping to hear.
6.explain:
“Listen, for I will speak of excellent things,”

Wisdom asks for a hearing and gives her reason. “Excellent things” are noble things, words of the highest worth. She does not keep lesser words for lesser people; the simple and the fools of 8:5 are offered her best.

“And from the opening of my lips will come right things;”

When she opens her mouth, what comes out is right, straight and upright. The contrast with the seductress is pointed. She made her words smooth (7:5, 21); Wisdom makes hers straight. Smooth words go down easily and lead astray; straight words may be harder to hear, but they lead to life.
6.notes: The Hebrew word behind “excellent things” is the plural of a word for a leader or prince, so Wisdom promises princely, noble words; the ESV and NASB render it “noble things.”

7.brief: Her mouth will speak truth, and wickedness is an abomination to her lips. Truthfulness belongs to her nature, so lying is something she finds detestable.
7.explain:
“For my mouth will speak truth;”

Wisdom’s speech is true. The Hebrew word for truth carries the sense of what is firm and reliable, what a person can lean on. Her words will hold the weight of a life built on them.

“Wickedness is an abomination to my lips.”

“Abomination” is the word Proverbs usually uses for what is detestable to the LORD, as in “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD” (11:1). Here wickedness is an abomination to Wisdom’s own lips. She shares the LORD’s revulsion at evil. Lying is not merely something she avoids; she finds it detestable, because truthfulness belongs to her nature.

8.brief: All her words are spoken in righteousness, with nothing crooked or perverse in them. Unlike the twisted speech of evil men and the flattery of the seductress, Wisdom’s words are straight through and through.
8.explain:
“All the words of my mouth are with righteousness;”

“All” leaves no exceptions. Every word Wisdom speaks is spoken in righteousness, in line with what is right before God. Her hearers do not have to sort through her words to find the trustworthy ones.

“Nothing crooked or perverse is in them.”

“Crooked” means twisted, and “perverse” means bent out of shape. The seductress’s method was all twisting: religion turned into an excuse in 7:14, adultery renamed love in 7:18, secrecy offered as safety in 7:19. Wisdom’s words have no twist in them at all. “All” at the start of the verse and “Nothing” at the start of this line close every gap through which deceit could enter.

9.brief: To the one who understands, her words are plain, and to those who find knowledge they are right. Wisdom is not obscure to an open heart; those willing to learn find her words clear and true.
9.explain:
“They are all plain to him who understands,”

Wisdom’s words are plain, straightforward and clear, to the one who understands. They are not a puzzle reserved for experts. A heart that is open and willing to learn finds them clear.

“And right to those who find knowledge.”

To those who find knowledge, her words are right, straight and true. The verse does not claim that every word of wisdom is equally easy for everyone; the book itself speaks of “an enigma” and of riddles (1:6). It says that the person who is willing to learn finds her words reliable, and that understanding grows as it is used. Clarity belongs to the willing heart.

10.brief: Wisdom urges her hearers to receive her instruction instead of silver and knowledge rather than choice gold. Given the choice between wealth and wisdom, the wise choose instruction.
10.explain:
“Receive my instruction, and not silver,”

Wisdom sets her instruction against money and asks her hearers to choose. “Instruction” is the word for discipline and training, including correction. Most people would gladly take silver and avoid correction. Wisdom says the opposite choice is the wise one.

“And knowledge rather than choice gold;”

“Choice gold” is the finest, most refined gold, and even that is worth less than knowledge. The verse does not promise silver and gold as a reward for choosing wisdom. It says that wisdom is worth more than they are, and that given the choice, the wise choose instruction.

11.brief: Wisdom is better than rubies, and nothing a person could desire compares with her. The verse echoes the earlier praise of wisdom (3:15), confirming that she is worth more than anything else a person could pursue.
11.explain:
“For wisdom is better than rubies,”

Rubies stand here for the most valuable jewels a person could own, and wisdom is better than them. The line echoes the father’s earlier praise: “She is more precious than rubies” (3:15). What the father said about wisdom in chapter 3, Wisdom now confirms in the middle of her own speech.

“And all the things one may desire cannot be compared with her.”

Nothing a person could want compares with wisdom: not wealth, not pleasure, not the luxuries the seductress described in 7:16–17. The comparison is total. Within Wisdom’s speech the verse speaks of wisdom as “her,” stating a principle before Wisdom resumes speaking as “I” in 8:12.
11.notes: The Hebrew word translated “rubies” names a precious stone or jewel that cannot be identified with certainty. Hebrew lexicons suggest coral or pearls, and the ESV and NASB render the word “jewels.”

12.brief: Wisdom introduces herself, “I, wisdom,” saying that she dwells with prudence and finds out knowledge and discretion. Good sense and sound judgment are her constant companions, so where wisdom is, practical skill for living is found as well.
12.explain:
“I, wisdom, dwell with prudence,”

Wisdom introduces herself by name: “I, wisdom.” She dwells with prudence; she lives with practical good sense as a constant companion under the same roof. Where wisdom is, sound judgment about real situations is found as well. Wisdom is not theory detached from life. It is skill for living God’s way, and prudence belongs to her household.

“And find out knowledge and discretion.”

She finds out knowledge and discretion, discovering them and bringing them to light. “Discretion” is the ability to plan a wise course and think ahead. Wisdom does not merely possess these things; she seeks them out and supplies them to those who listen. Her words echo the purpose of the whole book, which was written “To give prudence to the simple, To the young man knowledge and discretion” (1:4).

13.brief: The fear of the LORD is defined here as hating evil, and Wisdom names what she hates: pride, arrogance, the evil way, and the perverse mouth. A right view of God produces a settled hatred of evil, beginning with pride.
13.explain:
“The fear of the LORD is to hate evil;”

The book’s motto said that “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7). Here the fear of the LORD receives a moral definition: it is to hate evil. The fear of the LORD is a right view of God, seeing Him as He truly is in His holiness and goodness. A person who sees God rightly begins to see evil as God sees it, and to hate it.

“Pride and arrogance and the evil way”

Wisdom names what she hates, and pride comes first, named twice in “Pride and arrogance.” Pride is the direct opposite of fearing God, because it puts self in the place that belongs to God. “The evil way” is a whole course of life given over to wrong. The list recalls the things the LORD hates in 6:16–19, which also begin with pride.

“And the perverse mouth I hate.”

Wisdom also hates the perverse mouth, the twisted and deceitful speech of the worthless man in 6:12. Her hatred matches the LORD’s own. Those who walk with her come to share what she loves and what she hates, and pride is the first thing that has to go.

14.brief: Wisdom claims counsel and sound wisdom as her own, and says she is understanding and has strength. She does not merely give advice; she possesses the insight and power needed to carry it out.
14.explain:
“Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom;”

“Counsel” is advice, the ability to give a sound plan. “Sound wisdom” is practical effectiveness, the kind of wisdom that actually succeeds. Wisdom claims both as her own. She knows what should be done.

“I am understanding, I have strength.”

She does not merely have understanding; she is understanding. And she has strength, the power to carry out what she advises. Many people know what they should do but lack the strength to do it, and others have strength but no counsel. Wisdom has both the plan and the power. Isaiah describes the coming King in similar terms, with “The Spirit of counsel and might” resting on Him (Isaiah 11:2).

15.brief: By Wisdom kings reign and rulers decree what is just. Good government depends on her, and any ruler who governs justly does so through the wisdom God gives.
15.explain:
“By me kings reign,”

In the ancient world the king was the highest human authority. Wisdom says that kings reign by her. Every king who rules well does so through a wisdom he did not invent. Wisdom stands above the throne.

“And rulers decree justice.”

Rulers who make just laws do so by wisdom. To “decree” is to issue an ordinance, to set a rule in place, and just laws reflect the order God built into His world. The verse speaks of wisdom’s role in all just government, wherever it is found. It does not make every king in Proverbs a picture of Christ, though in the book’s fuller reading the Wisdom by whom kings reign is the One whom Scripture finally names “KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS” (Revelation 19:16).

16.brief: Princes, nobles, and all the judges of the earth also rule by her. Wisdom’s authority reaches every level of leadership, showing that all just rule depends on her.
16.explain:
“By me princes rule, and nobles,”

The list continues down the ranks of authority, princes and nobles. Every level of leadership depends on wisdom.

“All the judges of the earth.”

“All the judges of the earth” extends wisdom’s authority to every land and every court. No ruler anywhere can govern justly apart from the wisdom God gives, whether or not he acknowledges its source. The verse humbles human power. Kings and judges are not the final word; they are accountable to a wisdom above them.
16.notes: The Hebrew text followed by the ESV and NASB ends 8:16 with the word for “righteousness,” literally ‘all who judge righteousness,’ which lies behind the ESV’s ‘all who govern justly’ and the NASB’s ‘All who judge rightly.’ The NKJV and KJV read “earth,” which reflects a different reading of the Hebrew text at this point. The sense of just rule is the same on either reading.

17.brief: Wisdom says, “I love those who love me,” and those who seek her diligently will find her. Love is returned and seeking is rewarded, and in the light of the New Testament these are the words of Christ, who is found by those who seek Him.
17.explain:
“I love those who love me,”

Wisdom now speaks of love. She is not a cold principle but one who returns love. In the plain sense of the poem, love for wisdom is met by wisdom’s own favor, and the person who values her receives more of her. In the light of the New Testament these words are heard as Christ’s own. Jesus said, “he who loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him and manifest Myself to him” (John 14:21). His love comes first, and those who answer it find Him making Himself known to them more and more.

“And those who seek me diligently will find me.”

To seek diligently is to seek eagerly and earnestly, with focus. The promise is that such seeking is never in vain. The seductress used the same language for her pursuit of the young man in 7:15, but her seeking ended in death; this seeking ends in finding the one who gives life. Earlier the father said that wisdom must be sought “as silver” and searched for “as for hidden treasures” (2:4). At the book’s deeper level, seeking wisdom with that intensity is seeking Christ, “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).
17.notes: “Seek me diligently” and “Diligently to seek” in 7:15 translate the same Hebrew verb; the KJV renders it here ‘seek me early.’

18.brief: Riches and honor are with Wisdom, enduring riches joined with righteousness. Her wealth lasts because it is bound up with right living, unlike riches that fly away (23:5); the saying commends wisdom’s true and lasting goods rather than promising every wise person a fortune.
18.explain:
“Riches and honor are with me,”

Wisdom now speaks of what she gives. Riches and honor are found with her, in her company. The father said the same of wisdom earlier: “In her left hand riches and honor” (3:16). These are real goods, provision and a good name.

“Enduring riches and righteousness.”

Her riches are enduring, and they are joined to righteousness. Riches gained apart from righteousness do not last, for “riches certainly make themselves wings” (23:5). The riches Wisdom gives last because they belong to a life lived rightly before God. Like the book’s other sayings about blessing, the verse states what is generally true in God’s world and commends wisdom’s lasting goods. It does not promise a fortune to every wise person, and Proverbs elsewhere warns against trusting in riches. Jesus had all wisdom and lived without wealth. The riches Wisdom offers are measured first by righteousness and the favor of God.

19.brief: Her fruit is better than fine gold and her revenue better than choice silver. What Wisdom produces in a life is worth more than the finest wealth.
19.explain:
“My fruit is better than gold, yes, than fine gold,”

Wisdom speaks of her fruit, what she produces in a life. Gold and fine gold are the market’s measure of value, but Wisdom’s fruit is better. Fruit is alive and keeps growing; gold only sits in a treasury.

“And my revenue than choice silver.”

“Revenue” is yield or income, what comes in from a harvest or an investment. Wisdom’s yield is better than the finest silver. What she grows in a person, character, righteousness and peace with God and others, is worth more than any income. The verse continues the comparison of 8:10–11 and keeps it at the level of value. It is not a promise of wealth.

20.brief: Wisdom walks in the way of righteousness, in the middle of the paths of justice. She never strays from what is right, and those who follow her walk the same road.
20.explain:
“I traverse the way of righteousness,”

Wisdom does not stand beside the road pointing; she walks it. To “traverse” is to walk along and travel. Her road is the way of righteousness, the road of right living before God, and those who follow her walk where she walks.

“In the midst of the paths of justice,”

She walks in the middle of the paths of justice, not along the edge. The young man of chapter 7 walked “near her corner” (7:8); Wisdom walks in the center of the right road. The line ends with a comma because the sentence continues into 8:21, which states the purpose of her walking there. The riches of 8:18 and the inheritance of 8:21 are found along this road and not apart from it.

21.brief: Her purpose is to give an inheritance to those who love her and to fill their treasuries. These gifts come along the paths of righteousness just described, and like the book’s other outcome sayings, the verse describes the rich fruit of loving wisdom without guaranteeing material prosperity to everyone who does.
21.explain:
“That I may cause those who love me to inherit wealth,”

Wisdom states her purpose: to give an inheritance to those who love her. “Inherit” is the language of children, not of hired workers. What she gives is received as a gift, not earned as a wage. “Wealth” here means substance, what is real and solid.

“That I may fill their treasuries.”

She intends to fill their storehouses. These gifts come along the paths of righteousness described in 8:20. Like the book’s other outcome sayings, the verse describes the rich fruit of loving wisdom without guaranteeing material prosperity to everyone who does. Some of God’s wisest servants have been poor in this world, and their treasuries were filled with what cannot be stolen or lost. The verse speaks of real provision, but its measure of wealth is larger than money.
21.notes: The Hebrew word rendered “wealth” is the ordinary word for “there is.” This verse is the only place in the Old Testament where it serves as a noun meaning substance, what really exists, and the KJV renders it “substance.”

22.brief: Wisdom now speaks of her origin, saying the LORD possessed her at the beginning of His way, before His works of old. Wisdom has belonged to God from the very first, and since this Wisdom is revealed as the eternal Son, the verse must never be read as if the Son had a beginning (John 1:1).
22.explain:
“The LORD possessed me at the beginning of His way,”

Wisdom now speaks of her origin, and the poem moves from her call and her gifts to her place beside the LORD before anything was made. “The LORD possessed me” means that Wisdom belonged to the LORD and was His from the very first. “The beginning of His way” refers to the start of God’s activity in creating the world. God was never without His wisdom; before He made anything, Wisdom was already His.

“Before His works of old.”

“His works of old” are the works of creation, and Wisdom was there before them. The verse is poetry. It does not describe a moment when wisdom began; it declares that wisdom belongs to God from before all His works, as the next verse says plainly, “from everlasting” (8:23). Because the Wisdom who speaks here is revealed in the New Testament as the eternal Son, the verse must never be read as though the Son was created or had a beginning. John writes, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The Son is not one of God’s works. He is the One through whom they were made.
22.notes:
The Hebrew verb rendered “possessed” usually means to get or acquire, and in a few poetic passages it is used of God as the one who brings something into being, as when Genesis 14:19 calls Him “Possessor of heaven and earth.” Translations therefore differ here. The NKJV, ESV, NASB and KJV read “possessed”; the 1984 NIV has ‘brought me forth,’ the NLT “formed me,” and the AMP ‘created and possessed.’

The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, rendered the verb with a Greek word meaning “created.” In the fourth century Arius and his followers took the verse in that sense to argue that the Son was a created being. The church rejected that teaching at the Council of Nicaea in AD 325, confessing the Son as ‘begotten, not made.’

23.brief: She was established from everlasting, from the beginning, before there was ever an earth. Wisdom’s existence reaches back before creation into eternity, which fits the Son who shared the Father’s glory before the world was (John 17:5).
23.explain:
“I have been established from everlasting,”

“From everlasting” reaches back beyond time. Wisdom was established, set in place or appointed, from eternity. Nothing in creation is older. “Everlasting” is the language Scripture uses of God Himself.

“From the beginning, before there was ever an earth.”

“From the beginning” and “before there was ever an earth” press the same point from two directions. Wisdom did not appear partway through the story of the world; she was there before the story began. The line fits the Son who prayed, “glorify Me together with Yourself, with the glory which I had with You before the world was” (John 17:5). What Proverbs says of Wisdom in poetry, the New Testament says plainly of Christ: “He is before all things, and in Him all things consist” (Colossians 1:17).
23.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “established” is used elsewhere of installing a king, and here it means that Wisdom was set in place. It is rendered “set up” in the ESV and KJV, “appointed” in the NLT and the 1984 NIV, and “formed” in the current NIV.

24.brief: When there were no ocean depths and no springs overflowing with water, Wisdom was brought forth. The poem places her before the first features of creation, showing she was with God before anything was made.
24.explain:
“When there were no depths I was brought forth,”

The depths are the deep waters, the ocean deep that covered the earth at the beginning, when “darkness was on the face of the deep” (Genesis 1:2). Before they existed, Wisdom was brought forth. The phrase uses the language of birth, pictured poetically. It speaks of Wisdom’s origin in God and her closeness to Him. Applied to the eternal Son, “brought forth” may be connected with His eternal relation to the Father, the Son who is always the Son of the Father, but never with a start to His existence.

“When there were no fountains abounding with water.”

Fountains abounding with water are springs, the sources of water on the earth. They too came later. The poem moves through the oldest and deepest features of creation and places Wisdom before every one of them.
24.notes: The 1984 NIV (‘I was given birth’) and the AMP (“I was born”) make the birth language of “brought forth” explicit.

25.brief: Wisdom was brought forth before the mountains were settled in place and before the hills. Even the oldest and most lasting parts of the earth are younger than Wisdom.
25.explain:
“Before the mountains were settled,”

Mountains seem the most permanent things on earth; they stand when everything else changes. Before they were settled, sunk into their foundations and set in place, Wisdom was there.

“Before the hills, I was brought forth;”

The hills, too, are younger than Wisdom. The repeated “I was brought forth” of 8:24–25 frames this part of the poem. A psalm speaks of God Himself in similar terms: “Before the mountains were brought forth, Or ever You had formed the earth and the world, Even from everlasting to everlasting, You are God” (Psalm 90:2). Wisdom speaks of herself in the language Scripture uses for God’s own eternity.

26.brief: She was there while God had not yet made the earth, the fields, or the first dust of the world. The list reaches down to the smallest beginnings of creation, and Wisdom was before them all.
26.explain:
“While as yet He had not made the earth or the fields,”

The poem reaches down from mountains and hills to the earth itself and to the open fields where people would one day plant and harvest. None of them had yet been made.

“Or the primal dust of the world.”

“The primal dust” is the first dust, the most basic material of the land, the smallest beginnings of the earth. “The world” is the inhabited world, the earth as the home of people. Wisdom was there before even the dust existed. Man was later formed “of the dust of the ground” (Genesis 2:7), so Wisdom was before the very dust from which humanity would come.
26.notes: “World” here and “inhabited world” in 8:31 translate the same Hebrew word, a poetic word for the world as the place where people and creatures live.

27.brief: When the LORD prepared the heavens, Wisdom says, “I was there,” as He drew a circle on the face of the deep. She now speaks from the scene of creation itself, present as God set the boundaries of the world.
27.explain:
“When He prepared the heavens, I was there,”

The poem now moves from before creation to the act of creation itself. When the LORD prepared the heavens, setting the sky in place, Wisdom says, “I was there.” She speaks as an eyewitness of creation. The one who calls people at the crossroads in 8:2 was present when the heavens were established.

“When He drew a circle on the face of the deep,”

God drew a circle on the face of the deep, marking a boundary on the waters, the line of the horizon where sky meets sea. Job uses the same picture: “He drew a circular horizon on the face of the waters” (Job 26:10). Creation is described as an ordered work, with God setting limits and boundaries. “The face of the deep” recalls the first verses of Genesis, and out of what was formless God brought order while Wisdom looked on.

28.brief: Wisdom was present when He established the clouds above and strengthened the springs of the deep. Wisdom witnessed God setting both the skies and the waters below in their places.
28.explain:
“When He established the clouds above,”

To “establish” is to make firm. Clouds seem the least solid things in the sky, yet God set them in place and gave them their work of holding the rain. Even what looks weightless obeys His ordering.

“When He strengthened the fountains of the deep,”

The fountains of the deep are the springs that rise from beneath the earth. God strengthened them, setting them firmly so that they flow within their bounds. The verse pairs the waters above with the waters below, and Wisdom was present at both. Proverbs 3 said the same: “The LORD by wisdom founded the earth; By understanding He established the heavens” (3:19).

29.brief: As God gave the sea its limit so the waters would not overstep His command, and as He marked out the foundations of the earth, she was present. Creation is pictured as an ordered work, every part obeying God’s word, with Wisdom present at each step.
29.explain:
“When He assigned to the sea its limit,”

The sea, often in Scripture a picture of untamed power, was given a limit, a boundary it cannot cross. God speaks of the same act in Job: “When I fixed My limit for it, And set bars and doors” (Job 38:10).

“So that the waters would not transgress His command,”

The waters do not transgress His command; the sea obeys. “Transgress” is the language of crossing a line, the same idea Scripture uses of human sin. The sea keeps its boundary, while human beings cross theirs. The contrast is quiet but real: the Wisdom who calls people to keep God’s ways in 8:32 watched the sea keep God’s command.

“When He marked out the foundations of the earth,”

God marked out the foundations of the earth, like a builder laying out the lines for a building’s base. The earth rests on what God established. Wisdom was present at every stage of this ordered work, so the counsel she gives the simple comes from the one who saw how the world was put together.
29.notes: “Marked out” in 8:29, the verb in “drew a circle” in 8:27 and “decree” in 8:15 all translate the same Hebrew verb, which means to cut in or engrave, and so to mark out or to decree. The order God fixed in creation and the justice rulers are to decree are described with the same word.

30.brief: Then she was beside Him as a master craftsman, daily His delight, rejoicing always before Him. In the poem Wisdom works at God’s side with joy, and in the light of the New Testament this is the eternal Son, through whom all things were made and in whom the Father delights (Hebrews 1:2).
30.explain:
“Then I was beside Him as a master craftsman;”

“Then,” during all this work of creation, Wisdom was beside Him. The phrase pictures close partnership, standing at the Creator’s side. “As a master craftsman” presents Wisdom as a skilled worker sharing in God’s work, the architect beside the builder. The Hebrew word behind “master craftsman” is rare and its exact sense is debated, but the NKJV’s picture is of Wisdom at work alongside God as the world was made. In the light of the New Testament this is the eternal Son: “All things were made through Him” (John 1:3), and through Him the Father “made the worlds” (Hebrews 1:2). The identification rests on the New Testament’s testimony, not on the poem’s personification alone.

“And I was daily His delight,”

“Daily His delight” means that day after day God delighted in Wisdom. Before creation there was joy, delight between God and His Wisdom, and the work of creation was done in an atmosphere of love and gladness, not need. At the deeper level this is the Father’s delight in the Son. Jesus prayed, “You loved Me before the foundation of the world” (John 17:24), and at His baptism the Father said, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

“Rejoicing always before Him,”

Wisdom rejoiced continually in God’s presence. The delight was mutual: God delighted in Wisdom, and Wisdom rejoiced before God. The picture is of creation coming from the overflow of joy within God, a joy the Son has shared with the Father from eternity.
30.notes:
The Hebrew word rendered “master craftsman” is very rare, and it has been understood in two main ways. The NKJV, ESV and NASB take it as a skilled worker (ESV and NASB “master workman”; NLT “the architect”). The KJV reads ‘as one brought up with him,’ taking it as a child being raised, a reading found in some medieval Jewish interpreters. Each reading fits the scene of closeness and delight before God.

The Hebrew verb translated “rejoicing” can also mean to laugh or to play; the same verb describes children “Playing in its streets” (Zechariah 8:5). The word pictures Wisdom’s joy before God as free and glad.

31.brief: Wisdom rejoiced in God’s inhabited world, and her delight was with the sons of men. Her joy reaches past the mountains and seas to people, and this delight in humanity finds its fullest expression in the Son who came to dwell among us (John 1:14).
31.explain:
“Rejoicing in His inhabited world,”

Wisdom’s joy extends to the world God made, the inhabited world, the earth as a home for living creatures. She is glad in God’s creation. God saw that His work was “very good” (Genesis 1:31), and Wisdom rejoiced in it.

“And my delight was with the sons of men.”

Of everything in creation, Wisdom’s special delight was the sons of men, human beings. The same phrase opened her call in 8:4. She calls people because she delights in them. The Hebrew noun behind “delight” here, which means delight or enjoyment, is the same word used of God’s delight in Wisdom in 8:30: God delighted in Wisdom, and Wisdom delighted in humanity. In the light of the New Testament this delight finds its fullest expression in the Son, who did not merely watch the human race from a distance but became one of us: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

32.brief: Turning to her hearers, Wisdom says, “Now therefore, listen to me, my children,” for those who keep her ways are blessed. Everything she has said about her truth and her place beside God becomes the reason to listen to her now.
32.explain:
“Now therefore, listen to me, my children,”

“Now therefore” draws the conclusion from everything Wisdom has said. She has spoken of her truth, her gifts, her place with God before the world began and her presence at creation, and now she turns all of it into a reason to listen. “My children” is the father’s own address in 7:24, and Wisdom uses it to speak to her hearers as family. The one who stood beside the Creator speaks personally to those who will hear.

“For blessed are those who keep my ways.”

“Blessed” describes the happy, flourishing life that comes from walking with God. Those who keep Wisdom’s ways, who walk her paths and do not turn aside, are blessed. Her ways were described in 8:20, the way of righteousness and the paths of justice. Real happiness is found by walking those roads, not by throwing off God’s ways.

33.brief: She urges them to hear instruction and be wise and not to reject it. The call is simple and direct, because refusing instruction is the one thing that keeps a person from wisdom.
33.explain:
“Hear instruction and be wise,”

The call is simple and direct: hear instruction, and you will be wise. “Instruction” is the word for discipline and correction, the same word Wisdom set above silver in 8:10. Wisdom grows by listening, by receiving teaching and correction.

“And do not disdain it.”

To “disdain” is to refuse, to let go, to neglect. The danger is not always open rejection; it can be simply letting instruction slip away. The man of 5:12 hated instruction and came to ruin. Refusing instruction is the one thing that keeps a person from wisdom.

34.brief: Blessed is the person who listens to her, watching daily at her gates and waiting at the posts of her doors. The picture is of eager, daily devotion, like someone who waits at a door each morning, eager for it to open.
34.explain:
“Blessed is the man who listens to me,”

A second “blessed” follows. The blessed person listens to Wisdom, not occasionally but as a habit of life.

“Watching daily at my gates,”

“Watching daily” pictures someone who comes every day and waits at Wisdom’s gates, attentive and expectant. The word “daily” echoes 8:30, where Wisdom was “daily His delight.” As Wisdom was God’s daily delight, the blessed person makes Wisdom a daily pursuit.

“Waiting at the posts of my doors.”

Waiting at the posts of the doors is the picture of someone standing at a doorway, eager for it to open, as a servant waits at his master’s door or a friend waits for someone he loves. It describes eager, daily devotion. At the deeper level this is devotion to Christ, the Wisdom of God: a heart that loves to be near Him, not a rule prescribing a particular method. Wisdom came to the doors of the city in 8:3; now the blessed person comes to hers.

35.brief: For whoever finds Wisdom finds life and obtains favor from the LORD. The promise reaches its fulfillment in Christ, who is the life (John 14:6), and finding Him brings God’s favor.
35.explain:
“For whoever finds me finds life,”

“Whoever” opens the promise to anyone. To find Wisdom is to find life, the full and flourishing life God intends, lived in His favor. The promise is attached to a person: whoever finds me. In the light of the New Testament it reaches its fulfillment in Christ, who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). To find Him is to find life itself.

“And obtains favor from the LORD;”

The one who finds Wisdom also obtains favor from the LORD, His approval, kindness and blessing. Finding Wisdom brings a person into God’s delight; the Wisdom who was “daily His delight” (8:30) brings those who find her into the LORD’s favor. The semicolon at the end of the line sets this promise directly against the warning of 8:36.
35.notes: The words “obtains favor from the LORD” return in 18:22, “He who finds a wife finds a good thing, And obtains favor from the LORD,” and the book closes with the question “Who can find a virtuous wife?” (31:10). The language of finding links Wisdom at the start of the book with the wife of worth at its end.

36.brief: The one who sins against Wisdom wrongs his own soul, and all who hate her love death. The chapter ends with the two ways: rejecting Wisdom is finally self-destruction, a choice for death over life.
36.explain:
“But he who sins against me wrongs his own soul;”

The chapter closes with the other way. The Hebrew verb behind “sins against me” can also mean to miss, so the line can be understood as missing or failing to find Wisdom, the opposite of “finds me” in 8:35. The person who misses Wisdom, or turns against her, wrongs his own soul and does violence to himself. Turning from Wisdom never harms her; it harms the one who turns.

“All those who hate me love death.”

To hate Wisdom is, in effect, to love death. A person who rejects Wisdom may be reaching for some other good he wants at the moment, but the road he chooses ends in death. The chapter ends at the same fork in the road where it began in 8:2: life for those who find Wisdom, death for those who hate her. The same Wisdom whose delight was with the sons of men speaks this warning, because she wants them to live. In chapter 9 Wisdom’s house and table will be set beside Folly’s, and the choice will be put once more.
36.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “sins against me” is the common verb for sinning, and it can also mean to miss. The same verb describes the slingers of Judges 20:16, who could “sling a stone at a hair’s breadth and not miss.” Here the ESV and the 1984 NIV read ‘fails to find me,’ and the NLT “those who miss me injure themselves,” which brings out the contrast with “finds me” in 8:35.
